\[
\left|F\cap(\{i\}\times[m])\right|\leq2\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad
\left|F\cap(\{4\}\times[m])\right|\leq m-5,
\]
and
\[
\left|F\cap(\{1,2,3,4\}\times\{j\})\right|\leq1\quad(j\in[m]).
\]
For integers \(t\geq2\) and \(n\geq2\), let \(M(\mathbb Z/t\mathbb Z,n)\) denote the Moore space obtained from \(S^n\) by attaching one \((n+1)\)-cell along a map \(S^n\to S^n\) of degree \(t\). A wedge identifies chosen basepoints, and a wedge with zero summands is a point.

Determine the homotopy type of the geometric realization \(|K_m|\) for every \(m\geq7\), expressed as a finite wedge of spheres and Moore spaces, with every dimension, cyclic order, and multiplicity given explicitly as a function of \(m\).
</problem>

111	## 3. A contractible enlargement
112	
113	Let \(X_m\) be obtained by omitting the bound on row \(4\), while retaining the column bounds and the bounds of two on rows \(1,2,3\).
114	
115	Every facet of \(X_m\) occupies all \(m\) columns. It is specified by a function
116	\[
117	f:[m]\longrightarrow\{1,2,3,4\}
118	\]
119	using each of \(1,2,3\) at most twice.
120	
121	Order the facets by increasing number of entries different from \(4\), breaking ties arbitrarily. The first facet is the all-\(4\) simplex.
122	
123	Consider a later facet \(F\), and let \(T\) be its set of vertices outside row \(4\). Its intersection with the union of earlier facets is exactly
124	\[
125	\bigcup_{v\in T}(F\setminus\{v\}).
126	\tag{8}
127	\]
128	Indeed, replacing any \(v\in T\) by the row-\(4\) vertex in its column gives an earlier facet. Conversely, an earlier, distinct facet cannot agree with \(F\) at every vertex of \(T\): doing so would use at least as many non-\(4\) entries, and equality would force the two facets to coincide.

130	Since
131	\[
132	1\le |T|\le6<m,
133	\]
134	(8) is a nonempty proper union of facets of the boundary of a simplex, hence contractible. Attaching the next simplex therefore preserves homotopy type. Consequently,
135	\[
136	X_m\simeq *.
137	\tag{9}
138	\]

143	\cong H_{i+1}(X_m,K_m;\mathbb Z).

147	## 4. The small relative chain complex
148	
149	A relative face of \((X_m,K_m)\) has at least \(m-4\) row-\(4\) vertices.
150

152	\[
153	(U,A_1,A_2,A_3),
154	\]
155	where \(U\) is the set of unoccupied columns and \(A_i\) records the columns occupied in row \(i\). All remaining columns contain row-\(4\) vertices. Its conditions are
156	\[
157	|A_i|\le2,\qquad
158	|U|+|A_1|+|A_2|+|A_3|\le4.
159	\tag{11}
160	\]
161	Its dimension is \(m-|U|-1\).
162	
163	Let \(R^u\) be the free abelian group on these relative faces with \(|U|=u\). The relative boundary gives a complex
164	\[
165	R^0\longrightarrow R^1\longrightarrow R^2
166	\longrightarrow R^3\longrightarrow R^4.
167	\tag{12}

169	The rank of \(R^u\) is precisely \(b_u\): choose \(U\), choose the additional occupied columns, and color them with three colors, each used at most twice. The numbers of such colorings on \(a\le4\) positions are exactly
170	\[

175	\[
176	H^u(R^\bullet)=0\qquad(u\ge2).

180	### 4.1 Removing all three small-row bounds
181	
182	Let \(J_m\) be the join of \(m\) discrete four-point sets. Let \(A_m\subset J_m\) impose only the row-\(4\) bound \(m-5\).
183	
184	Both \(J_m\) and \(A_m\) are pure \((m-1)\)-dimensional shellable complexes. Here is a direct shelling argument for \(A_m\).
185	
186	Its facets are the functions \(f:[m]\to\{1,2,3,4\}\) with at most \(m-5\) entries equal to \(4\). Order them lexicographically, using \(1<2<3<4\). If \(g<f\), at the first differing coordinate \(j\) we have \(g(j)<f(j)\). Replacing just \(f(j)\) by \(g(j)\) is allowed: the replacement cannot increase the number of \(4\)'s. This supplies an earlier facet meeting \(f\) in a ridge containing \(f\cap g\), which is the shelling criterion.
187	
188	In particular, \(A_m\) and \(J_m\) have no reduced homology below degree \(m-1\). Since their relative chain complex has dimension at most \(m-1\),
189	\[
190	H_k(J_m,A_m;\mathbb Z)=0\qquad(k\ne m-1).

193	
194	Write \(F^\bullet\) for the version of (12) with no restrictions \(|A_i|\le2\). Equation (14) says

200	### 4.2 The quotient has only two groups

202	There is a short exact sequence of complexes
203	\[
204	0\longrightarrow R^\bullet\longrightarrow F^\bullet
205	\longrightarrow Q^\bullet\longrightarrow0.
206	\tag{16}
207	\]

209	A basis element of \(Q^\bullet\) violates at least one bound \(|A_i|\le2\). Because the total in (11) is at most four, it cannot violate two such bounds. Furthermore, it has \(|U|\le1\). Thus \(Q^\bullet\) has only \(Q^0,Q^1\).

211	Its differential \(Q^0\to Q^1\) is surjective over \(\mathbb Z\). To see this, a basis element of \(Q^1\) has three vertices in some row \(i\), and one unoccupied column \(j\). Fill \(j\) by a vertex in a different small row. The boundary of the resulting element of \(Q^0\), modulo \(R^\bullet\), is exactly the chosen basis element, with coefficient \(1\) or \(-1\). All other boundary terms satisfy every small-row bound.

243	* \(\tau_q\mid\tau_{q+1}\).

288	## 6. Why the homology determines the homotopy type here
289	
290	First, \(K_m\) is simply connected.
291	
292	It has the same \(1\)-skeleton as \(J_m\). The only triangles of \(J_m\) missing from \(K_m\) are monochromatic triples in one of the first three rows, and, when \(m=7\), monochromatic triples in row \(4\). The boundary of each missing triangle bounds a three-triangle disk in \(K_m\): cone it to a vertex in a different row and an unused column.
293	
294	Since \(J_m\) is simply connected, replacing missing triangles by these disks shows that \(K_m\) is simply connected.

296	Together with (18), the Hurewicz theorem now implies that \(K_m\) is \((m-4)\)-connected.

298	We use the following standard consequence of Hurewicz and Whitehead.
299	
300	**Two-degree lemma.** Suppose \(Y\) is a simply connected CW complex whose reduced homology is concentrated in degrees \(n,n+1\), where \(n\ge3\). Then
301	\[
302	Y\simeq
303	\bigvee^{a}S^n\vee
304	\bigvee^{b}S^{n+1}\vee
305	\bigvee_i M(\mathbb Z/t_i,n)
306	\]
307	whenever
308	\[
309	H_n(Y)\cong\mathbb Z^a\oplus\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z/t_i,
310	\qquad H_{n+1}(Y)\cong\mathbb Z^b.
311	\]
312	
313	For completeness, \(Y\) is \((n-1)\)-connected by Hurewicz. Represent the generators of \(H_n(Y)=\pi_n(Y)\) by maps of \(n\)-spheres. A torsion generator of order \(t\) extends across a degree-\(t\) attaching cell and therefore gives a map from \(M(\mathbb Z/t,n)\). The next-degree Hurewicz homomorphism
314	\(\pi_{n+1}(Y)\to H_{n+1}(Y)\) is surjective, so the free generators in that degree are also represented by spheres. The resulting map from the stated wedge to \(Y\) is an integral homology equivalence between simply connected CW complexes, hence a homotopy equivalence.

316	Apply this with \(n=m-3\ge4\) and (21). This proves (5).
